yearPlan.notice: Generated by scripts/compile-year-plan.mjs; edit the source planning documents, then npm run records. Allocations are proposals, not mastery.

chapters.title: 1. I can belong and contribute
chapters.journey: Arrival, invitation and a supported first responsibility at Sunday Markets.
chapters.carry: Knows how to act, seek help and resume; provisional aspiration, first useful contribution.

chapters.title: 2. I can choose an opportunity
chapters.journey: Meets advice/support, compares futures and crosses a threshold through an application.
chapters.carry: Source judgement and a reasoned application; a fictional role and commitments.

chapters.title: 3. My plans can change
chapters.journey: Encounters external change; investigates and adapts without being blamed for circumstances.
chapters.carry: Better alternatives, decision model and revised fictional budget.

chapters.title: 4. We can make work better
chapters.journey: Learns with others, takes initiative and contributes to a shared decision.
chapters.carry: Communication and collaboration evidence; a justified community proposal.

chapters.title: 5. I can show what I know
chapters.journey: Pauses, consolidates and demonstrates readiness; no manufactured story crisis for revision.
chapters.carry: Feedback, catch-up and a secure Unit 3 foundation.

chapters.title: 6. I can participate responsibly
chapters.journey: New role, interview, workplace expectations, rights and culture broaden the first idea of success.
chapters.carry: Observed communication, source-grounded conditions, values comparison and a small learning plan.

chapters.title: 7. I can respond and renew
chapters.journey: Handles feedback and concerns, seeks support, learns and applies something new.
chapters.carry: Improvement/recovery plan, justified advice pathway, completed CPD cycle.

chapters.title: 8. I can choose my next direction
chapters.journey: Return with learning: explains changed aspirations and applies capability elsewhere.
chapters.carry: Selected evidence and a provisional future; plural success, not a wealth ranking.

world.title: Environment and buildings
world.role: A community with homes, employers and services. Home Base supports planning; a Jobs Centre/advice service supports research, applications and later transitions; community services support shared decisions. No Megatrends or Initiative building is required. Exact service integration remains to design.

world.title: Avatar Studio and identity
world.role: Optional personalisation or ready-made avatar; provisional aspirations can change. Appearance and gaming skill do not determine learning access or achievement.

world.title: Earnings, saving and shop
world.role: First pay makes choice visible; later fictional budgets create trade-offs. Essential support is free. Money, purchases and badges are engagement/progression signals, not marks.

world.title: Community and tax
world.role: Simulated earnings can help explain shared services; formal class-investment work comes later. No universal rate, treasury integration or automatic promotion is locked. A teacher-held fictional fund is enough for planning.

world.title: Global possibilities
world.role: Wider labour-market comparisons are curriculum in Unit 3. Global multiplayer, trade and cross-school identity remain deferred; these are different meanings of “global”.

world.title: Disrepair → Growth → Flourishing
world.role: Environmental development can show shared change. It is not the hero cycle, individual capability scale or a fixed calendar of earned upgrades. No week below forces a world-stage switch.

weeks.focus: CE-EXP-V2-00 plus existing **Live Music & Sunday Markets**: arrival, 2D helper selection and a supported Market quick win are one opening experience. Include a light changing-world/megatrends encounter.
weeks.objectives: Operational: locate role/help, make a change, recognise an effect, leave/resume. I/P: U3-EB-01–03; I: U3-NOW-01–03 and U3-ES-COM-04. Separate T/P: U3-ES-DIG-02. No full megatrends or initiative coverage claim.
weeks.mode: World + accessible guided alternative; Teach for fictional profile safety (06). Ch. 2 pp. 24–31 and Ch. 6 pp. 140–149 support short explanations, not a worksheet dump.
weeks.evidence: Can explain the role and effect with support and notice how a change affects work; observe adult-rescue points. Safety case: identify risk and safer action. Interest/usability/reward remain separate from mastery.
weeks.gaps: Reuse latest Sunday Markets/00/06. 2D portraits load only the chosen static 3D helper. Reviewable slice design; full teaching, picker implementation and learning acceptance are unverified. Preserve current live Echo task order separately.

weeks.focus: **02: Which future should I trust?** Advice/service encounter comparing sources and possible roles. Establish a starter plan before a major shock.
weeks.objectives: T/P/A: U3-LWE-01–03; U3-ES-DIG-01, U3-ES-CRIT-01–03. T/P: U3-ES-PROB-01–02, U3-ES-TIME-01. Compare growth and jobs across locations; distinguish evidence from assertion and bias.
weeks.mode: World hook → Teach + Dedicated research; fictional or curated source alternatives.
weeks.evidence: Compare credible/current sources, include all labour-market categories and explain limitations; generate own questions/options. Teacher checks reasoning.
weeks.gaps: Reuse 02 and relevant Financing My Future research. Labour-market facts need current sources at authoring. New practice for questioning is a proposed addition to 02, not a changed canonical mapping.

weeks.focus: **01: The opportunity I might miss**, with **06: A public profile causes a problem**. Seek work and communicate suitability.
weeks.objectives: T/P/A, As?: U3-CB-01–06; U3-ES-COM-01–02, U3-ES-DIG-03–04, U3-ES-TIME-01. R/A: U3-ES-DIG-02, U3-ES-CRIT-03. Cover online/written/verbal routes and SAO/STAR/CAR.
weeks.mode: Teach/worked examples + Dedicated documents + Observed verbal response; service return to world.
weeks.evidence: Ad requirements matched to a relevant cover letter and structured response; changed-ad check tests adaptation. Practise electronic communication using approved/mock systems.
weeks.gaps: Reuse 01/06, CE-PILOT-01 teaching pattern and school Task 5 components; verify all techniques, not SAO alone. Résumé only as required/contextually useful. Two weeks is tight; feedback continues in consolidation. Formal Unit 4 interview process stays later.

weeks.focus: **03: The town changes overnight** with **05: My plan no longer adds up**. A changed work situation makes sources, risk and finance matter.
weeks.objectives: T/P/A, As?: U3-NOW-01–03; U3-PM-01–05; U3-ES-PROB-01–03. T/P: U3-ES-TIME-03; P: U3-ES-DIG-04; R/A: U3-LWE-01–03, U3-ES-CRIT-01–03, U3-ES-TIME-01.
weeks.mode: Bounded world change → Teach + Dedicated source/case comparison and spreadsheet budget; supported options.
weeks.evidence: Explain trend → work impact; independently generate alternatives; use and evaluate a decision model; revise a fictional budget with contingency and help pathway.
weeks.gaps: Reuse 03/05 and Financing My Future. One scenario cannot teach four megatrends, all life events, risks and six finance strategies: add concise comparison cases/teaching. No real family finance/health data. This is the highest Unit 3 content load.

weeks.focus: **04: Our team is about to let someone down**. Move from supported first contribution to purposeful teamwork, initiative and inclusion.
weeks.mode: Teach + Observed team task with individual roles; World consequence or equivalent case.
weeks.evidence: Each learner contributes reliably, listens/checks meaning and considers others; explain all initiative benefits and an inclusive response. Teacher sees body language/tone, not just selected dialogue.
weeks.gaps: Reuse 04, market Initiative reference/2C where suitable. Market badge does not close these points. Short individual alternatives plus planned interaction for missed observations; no popularity score.

weeks.focus: **07: What should our town fund?** Compact synthesis of already taught learning, not a new project course.
weeks.objectives: A/R: U3-ES-TEAM-04, U3-ES-DIG-04, U3-ES-CRIT-02, U3-ES-PROB-03, U3-PM-05. R/P: U3-ES-COM-01–04.
weeks.mode: Teacher-held fictional fund; short proposal/presentation/spreadsheet; World feedback optional.
weeks.evidence: Justify cost/access/work trade-offs; explain how others' evidence affected the decision. Assess reasoning separately from the winning vote.
weeks.gaps: Reuse 07; all listed points taught before this row. No functioning treasury, voting backend or built upgrade required. If compressed, fold the synthesis into 04/05 rather than use the protected reserve.

weeks.focus: Consolidation, absence recovery, feedback, Unit 3 response practice and EST preparation/administration at the actual school window. No new mandatory story arc.
weeks.objectives: R/P/A; As? school response/catch-up; **EST assesses only the year's nominated U3 content**. Diagnostic revisit of all U3 strands; targeted reteaching, not a promise to reassess all 43 points.
weeks.mode: Retained Dedicated CORE/TERM/VTCS/BOSS, memory cards/arcade where suitable; Teach for gaps; formal EST separate.
weeks.evidence: Recall plus explanation/application under appropriate conditions; teacher distinguishes revision scores from independently demonstrated capability.
weeks.gaps: Keep three flexible weeks in the allocation. This is not a confirmed EST date. If EST falls earlier, move relevant teaching and preparation before it and preserve remaining catch-up space. 2027 EST file located; highlighted subset and CORE mapping still need visual verification.

weeks.focus: **08: The interview becomes real**. Prepare for a new role. Launch a small **10** learning-needs/CPD thread after feedback so development can occur over time.
weeks.objectives: T/P/A, As?: U4-CB-01–02, U4-ES-COM-01–04. T/P: U4-ES-TIME-01–03. I/T/P: U4-LWE-01–03 and U4-ES-DIG-01, U4-ES-CRIT-01–02 for a modest learning need.
weeks.mode: Teach + Dedicated preparation + Observed interview; practice across formats; accessible school-approved alternative.
weeks.evidence: Know seven interview types and five process stages; perform relevant communication. Identify a need, select a realistic learning opportunity and schedule it.
weeks.gaps: Reuse 08 and school Video Interview; one-way video alone does not cover understanding of all formats. Actual performance/recording conditions await school outline; default teacher observation avoids unnecessary new video storage.

weeks.focus: **12, first pass: Something at work is not right**. Conditions and legislation explain a fictional work concern.
weeks.objectives: T/P/A, As?: U4-NOW-01–02; I/T: U4-NOW-03–04; T/P: U4-ES-DIG-02, U4-ES-PROB-01–03. R/A: U4-ES-DIG-01, U4-ES-CRIT-01–02.
weeks.mode: Teach + Dedicated current official-source enquiry; supported case/advice service.
weeks.evidence: Explain the purpose of each named Act; use one relevant award to check all eight condition categories; generate questions, alternatives and a reasoned next step.
weeks.gaps: Reuse 12 and Workplace Induction components. Inspect current legislation/award sources when authoring; no rates or legal advice invented. Introduce safe help-seeking now, deepen grievances later.

weeks.focus: **11: Two workplaces, two ways of living**. Compare culture, contribution and values without one ideal lifestyle.
weeks.objectives: T/P/A, As?: U4-EB-01–04, U4-ES-TEAM-01–04, U4-ES-DIG-03–04, U4-ES-CRIT-03. R/P: U4-ES-COM-01–04, U4-ES-TIME-01–03.
weeks.mode: Teach + Observed collaborative comparison; Dedicated documents/presentation/spreadsheet and mock electronic message.
weeks.evidence: Explain four culture types, seven characteristics and three alignment benefits; justify alternatives and demonstrate individual contribution.
weeks.gaps: Reuse 11 and school response material; two workplaces alone cannot represent four types—add short vignettes. No collection of personal values profiles required; character-based choices allowed.

weeks.focus: **09: Feedback I did not want to hear**. Make improvement possible; choose a resilience model and begin a review cycle.
weeks.objectives: T/P/A: U4-PM-01–03, U4-CB-03–04. R/A: U4-ES-COM-04, U4-ES-TIME-01–03; revisit during W27–30.
weeks.mode: Teach/model + Observed mentor/review conversation; concise fictional case alternatives.
weeks.evidence: Handle feedback with clarification, analysis and action; explain performance-management roles and apply a resilience model.
weeks.gaps: Reuse 09 and school response material. One week only launches the cycle; later checkpoints are essential. Review all change categories; not a personality/mental-health measure.

weeks.focus: **12, second pass: seek advice and act**. Transfer the earlier rights knowledge to a different concern and appropriate process.
weeks.objectives: T/P/A, As?: U4-NOW-03–04; R/A: U4-NOW-01–02, U4-ES-DIG-02, U4-ES-PROB-01–03, U4-ES-CRIT-01–02.
weeks.mode: Teach + Dedicated enquiry + teacher-supported case response/advice role-play; no real disclosures.
weeks.evidence: Distinguish all protocol/grievance categories, use current sources and justify a proportionate process. Explain what changes with a different issue.
weeks.gaps: Continue 12/Workplace Induction, not an automatic second graded task. Safe fictional cases, private support option and no compulsory reenactment of harassment.

weeks.focus: **10: The next opportunity needs something new**, with **09** follow-up. Complete the learning begun after interviews; apply and share it.
weeks.objectives: T/P/A: U4-LWE-01–03, U4-ES-DIG-01, U4-ES-CRIT-01–02. R/A: U4-PM-01–03, U4-CB-03–04, U4-ES-TIME-01–03, U4-ES-DIG-03–04. As? investigation if selected in the outline.
weeks.mode: Dedicated small learning opportunity + application in changed case/work task + brief sharing; mentor support.
weeks.evidence: Show need → participation → reflection → application → sharing, with teacher check of improvement/transfer. A purchased course or plan alone is insufficient.
weeks.gaps: Adapt school Learning for Life; keep Unit 4 placement. School extract emphasises planning/reflecting: explicitly retain applying and sharing. CPD time must fit existing work, not a second hidden course.

weeks.focus: **Look back, then look ahead**; existing yearArc payoff, details still to design. Consolidate, recover absences, finish feedback and select evidence of changed capability.
weeks.objectives: R/A across U4 and purposeful U3 retrieval; As? only approved unfinished sampling. No new content dependency or compulsory extra portfolio assessment.
weeks.mode: Teach for targeted gaps + changed-context task/discussion and selected existing work; optional world celebration.
weeks.evidence: Explain a changed future choice with evidence; demonstrate transfer to an unfamiliar ad, budget, feedback or workplace case as appropriate. Separate aspiration, enjoyment and achievement.
weeks.gaps: Two flexible weeks protected. Reuse work already produced; no new life-history collection or composite success score. Optional 13 discoveries must not consume essential recovery time.

rows.title: the concept of career adaptability

content: Career adaptability is the capacity to respond effectively to changes and challenges throughout working life. Three essential elements are flexibility, which allows plans and approaches to change; ongoing learning, which keeps skills relevant; and proactive career preparation, which anticipates opportunities and challenges.

The source applies adaptability to new roles or sectors, changed tasks/technology/responsibilities, and labour-market shifts. Its career-life-cycle discussion considers entry, growth, consolidation and change, with questions about capability, training access, values, affordability, family and work–life balance.
distinctions: A qualification alone is insufficient when roles and conditions change. The life-cycle stages are a reflection model, not fixed ages or a universal sequence.
Opportunity cost is the next-best option forgone when another is chosen.

rows.title: the concept of a growth industry

content: A growth industry is developed in the source as an industry with increasing employment. The explanation combines industry classification, measured increases over time and structural/cyclical causes. Historical comparisons show that apparent growth depends on the chosen period and on headcount versus percentage change.

Organic growth is explained more specifically as employment arising from continuing economic/social development and population expansion, maturation and ageing. Regular demand for education, health, personal care, construction and other services can generate linked work opportunities.
distinctions: Organic growth is one mechanism supporting industry employment; it is not a complete definition of every growth industry.
Employment size, workforce share, growth rate and future projection are different measures. National growth may conceal local or sub-sector decline.

rows.title: advantages and disadvantages of seeking employment in strong growth, average growth and negative growth industries

content: Strong, average and negative industry growth need to be considered alongside the kind and location of opportunities. The source develops structural change, which persistently alters industry composition or work; cyclical change, which follows expansion and contraction in economic activity; and demographic demand for services.

Useful comparison dimensions include entry and apprenticeship access, required skills, security, full-time prospects, casual or contract arrangements, regional concentration and indirect employment. An industry with more jobs does not automatically provide secure or suitable work, while local or specialist opportunities can differ from the aggregate.
distinctions: Absolute and percentage growth can rank industries differently; a chosen time horizon can change the apparent direction.
Industry appeal and growth are separate from job quality and personal pathway fit.

rows.title: the concept of initiative

content: Initiative is taking action without being told, using resourcefulness, problem-solving and a desire to improve work. It involves noticing a need or opportunity and responding proactively, rather than waiting for instructions on every task.

The source links initiative with motivation, independence, learning, communication, leadership and accepting responsibility. These are associated ideas, not fourteen separately defined requirements. Initiative is one of six overlapping enterprise-characteristic sets alongside adaptability, problem-solving, managed risk-taking, resilience and critical/creative thinking.
distinctions: Personal enterprise also occurs in social, community and educational settings; it is broader than running a business.
Initiative is compatible with teamwork and with checking authority, safety and readiness.

rows.title: the concept of megatrends

content: A trend is a pattern in how something changes over time, affecting society, culture, values or behaviour. A megatrend is a large global force producing sustained transformation in life, work and participation, sometimes across decades.

The source contrasts short- and long-term trends and domestic and global change, then identifies four curriculum megatrends: economic power shifts, demographic shifts, impactful technology and climate change. These forces help explain why tasks, skill needs, work settings and employment opportunities may change.
distinctions: The seven contextual trend categories on p. 140 are background, not seven extra megatrend requirements.
An isolated change at one workplace needs a connection to a wider sustained force before it illustrates a megatrend.

rows.title: importance of recognising and adjusting for diversity within a workplace

content: Workplace diversity includes different backgrounds, experiences, capabilities and needs among staff and external stakeholders. The source’s range extends beyond ethnicity to language, age, sex/gender, Indigeneity, religion, family status, disability and other differences.

Recognising diversity means understanding differing experience, skill, perspective and need. Adjusting means making practical changes that support and respect those differences. Inclusion can support fairness, engagement, motivation, retention and broader problem-solving; ignoring difference can contribute to misunderstanding, conflict, poor morale and discrimination concerns.
distinctions: Equal employment opportunity is presented as fair work-related access and protection from discrimination/harassment. Affirmative action is presented as positive organisational policy to attract, develop and retain underrepresented groups.
Recognising difference is separate from putting inclusive adjustments into practice.

rows.title: the concept of resilience

content: Resilience means adapting to adversity, recovering after setbacks and continuing purposeful action. The source considers personal life, workplace demands and the transition from school to further study or work.

Responses include maintaining realistic expectations, learning from failure, managing stress, organising commitments, seeking support, sustaining relationships and setting workable goals. Workplace examples add adaptability and initiative; transition examples include exploring options and managing rejection.
distinctions: Growth mindset is associated with resilience in the text but is not the same concept. Emotional intelligence is supporting context, explicitly not an additional curriculum dot point.

rows.title: the concept of lifelong learning

content: Lifelong learning is varied study and training continued throughout a career, beyond school and an initial qualification. Workers maintain knowledge, develop new skills, specialise or reskill as technology, industries, regulation, personal responsibilities and goals change.

The chapter presents entry, growth, consolidation and change as possible career phases. Development need not be a straight upward path: sideways moves or a less demanding role may suit values and later goals. Learning to learn means recognising opportunities and building the capacity and willingness to use them.
distinctions: Knowledge concerns what a person knows; skill concerns how to perform. Formal/informal learning and on/off-the-job learning describe different dimensions and can overlap.

rows.title: the concept and importance of enterprise culture

content: For the retained Year 12 concept, enterprise culture means shared workplace values, beliefs, attitudes, standards and behaviours shaping how people interact and work. Page 210 clarifies that every organisation has a culture, which may be positive, negative or indifferent.

Culture influences decisions, responsibility, responses to problems, recognition and treatment of people. A supportive culture can foster engagement, communication, teamwork and retention; poor culture can contribute to conflict, low morale, unfair treatment and poor service. Time, cost, short-term pressures, bureaucracy and resistance can constrain improvement.
distinctions: Formal culture appears in policies, structures and standards; informal culture appears in everyday habits, peer advice and modelling. Stated commitments can differ from lived practice. “Enterprising” quality specifically concerns initiative, innovation and proactive improvement.

stages.title: Use feedback to grow
stages.decision: How do I know how I am doing and make a useful improvement?
stages.teaching: Performance-management purposes and all five feedback-handling strategies, including fairness, emotional processing, evidence and a manageable action plan.
stages.application: Receive specific fictional/low-stakes task feedback, ask questions, agree a goal, try the improvement and revisit it in a later activity.
stages.product: A small goal-and-review record plus observed changed practice; distinguish feedback, performance management, recognition and support.
stages.later: This launches the need for CPD and gives a concrete starting point for J10 learning and change.
stages.limit: A plan alone is not an improvement cycle. Recognition need not be money, and accepting unfair feedback is not the learning aim.

stages.purpose: Use specific feedback and evidence to improve a contribution.

stages.title: Adapt, learn and move forward
stages.decision: What can I do when work or life changes, and what should I learn next?
stages.teaching: Resilience and illustrative models; lifelong learning and benefits; all five CPD elements; responses to unemployment, restructuring, promotion and feedback/review.
stages.application: A previously introduced megatrend now changes tasks or opportunities. Compare safe fictional career situations, then complete a bounded learn, use and share cycle within normal class work.
stages.product: A revised feasible pathway plus actual participation, reflection, application and sharing evidence from a small learning activity; explain how chosen supports help.
stages.later: Return to the original direction, budget, workplace criteria and evidence portfolio; choose the next step rather than imply one fixed adult life path.
stages.limit: Resilience is not compliance, diagnosis or a personality score. A proposed course is not completed CPD; neither retraining nor resilience guarantees employment.

portfolio.cadence: One short reflection per teaching week, using the actual school calendar when known; no invented dates or number of weeks.
prompts: Which employability skill did I use?
What example or evidence shows this?
What did I learn, improve, or want to try next?
portfolio.coverage: Ensure each of the 21 skills receives an explicit teaching encounter at least once in each unit, with development/practice throughout. A first-teach tick is a checkpoint, not permission to stop teaching the skill for the rest of the unit.
boundaries: A student log is not proof that explicit teaching occurred; the teacher records that separately.
A reflective claim is not automatically observed performance or mastery; link a concrete example/artifact when appropriate.
Logged evidence is not automatically formally assessed. Only link assessment after the real task, criterion and relevant evidence are verified.
One reflection can refer to a shared activity, but a group output alone does not prove each learner performed every skill.
No sensitive personal disclosure is required; classroom, fictional-case or work-simulation examples are sufficient.
portfolio.accessibility: Allow concise written, oral/audio or teacher-scribed reflection under school arrangements; assess the relevant skill rather than typing volume.
portfolio.integration: Proposed MyLife portfolio home and Stats summary of the same existing entries; preserve the existing teacher class view. MyLife My Work is currently a separate store; weekly tracking, record adapter and account/identity integration are not built here.

decisions.rationale: An accessible first job can precede a settled career goal and supplies concrete examples for later choices. Keep its hook but add explicit teaching and independent later application.
preserve: Mobile prepaid collection versus walk-up order/pay
Student observes, asks, tries, checks and hands over
$20 gross / $2 game tax / $18 net crew pass, independent of success and retries
change: Do not mark every initiative behaviour or skill complete from the existing queue
Add case coverage for missing initiative behaviours and stakeholder benefits
In the return, allow learner-generated options, authentic questions, role evidence and a changed constraint
decisions.limits: Not runtime-verified, not formal assessment, not evidence of a real tax rate or reward for correctness

decisions.rationale: Make source judgement and LMI support actual pathway decisions rather than a disconnected data hunt.
change: Range of jobs and all six LMI categories

decisions.rationale: Make global forces visible early, then let one recur as changed workplace tasks and later learning needs.
change: Work setting versus employment arrangement versus occupation demand
Do not use one shop change as proof of a global force

decisions.rationale: Applications become a purposeful response to a researched option, using genuine taster or other experience as evidence.
Retain useful application resources; replace calendar-first placement with a meaningful opportunity decision.
Merge source enquiry with LMI and future-work decisions; avoid duplicate Nora/Dev tasks.
Separate early trends, personal risk choices and later change; one changed-work activity cannot carry all of these concepts.
Use the brief paid taster then fuller team/inclusion/initiative transfer rather than an isolated late skills block.
Separate life-event breadth from the finance model while keeping consequences linked.
Place digital footprint/privacy with application and workplace decisions; use fictional accounts, not a real-profile audit.
A separate grand proposal is not automatically worth its time. Use compact synthesis/transfer within existing work unless the actual school assessment needs a distinct proposal.
Retain interview practice but add breadth and full interactive process; no seven-recording requirement.
Begin a genuine feedback/improvement cycle before later change and resilience; do not pretend one encounter proves improvement over time.
Complete a small CPD cycle, not a future learning plan only; retain Unit 4 formal teaching home.
Culture and values inform a workplace choice before entry, then are tested against lived practice.
Preview rights/conditions before commitment, teach full depth at the terms/induction clinic, then revisit consultation and redundancy during change.

tabs.label: Student experience
tabs.intro: Main steps beside actual implementation evidence, intended pedagogy and what a teacher would check. Missing captures remain visible as evidence gaps.

rows.title: 01 · Arrive at Sunday Markets
rows.action: Enter the actual 3D market and find Juniper Kitchen.
rows.pedagogy: Situate the first work problem in a recognisable place and give the learner a clear first contact.
rows.outcome: Know where to begin and who can authorise work.
rows.evidence: Navigation and arrival are participation, not initiative evidence.
rows.limits: Corrected exterior supplied in Library version2 and visually inspected. Navigation/arrival is not learning evidence; local owner verification is not live release acceptance.
rows.source: Repaired isolated source48a0fdb; Library review version2; exit/re-entry1280/854/390px.

rows.title: 02 · Meet Mara and Sam
rows.action: Hear the brief: phone orders are prepaid and collect by showing the order; walk-ups order/pay at the counter. Sam packs.
rows.pedagogy: Make roles, customer routes and the agreed task explicit before asking for a decision.
rows.outcome: Explain the difference between ordering and collection and who does what.
rows.evidence: Ask the learner to restate the agreed job and identify a question.
rows.limits: Following an assigned task alone is prompted action; do not label it spontaneous initiative.
rows.source: playable-3d/market-initiative.mjs; visual briefing in supplied review

rows.title: 03 · Investigate before changing anything
rows.action: Observe the queue, ask Mara/Sam/customers, and check information before choosing an action.
rows.pedagogy: Create a reason to seek information and challenge the first assumption.
rows.outcome: Justify a useful question or observation.
rows.evidence: Record what the learner noticed, what they asked and whether a prompt was used.
rows.limits: The game provides a supported investigation; independence needs separate observation.
rows.source: Market state and interaction source; step-specific screenshot requested

rows.title: 04 · Propose a safe trial
rows.action: Discuss an arrangement or another useful action with Mara. Check role limits, packing and the walkway; agree permission.
rows.pedagogy: Connect constructive initiative with communication, responsibility and a bounded test.
rows.outcome: Explain the action, its reason and a safety/permission limit.
rows.evidence: A specific proposal and rationale; distinguish independent choice from offered options.
rows.limits: Moving Sam into another role is not evidence of helping him. Seeking responsibility includes training and agreed limits.
rows.source: playable-3d/market-initiative.mjs: stock/sign/crew/help/training actions

rows.title: 05 · Watch the next customers
rows.action: Try the authorised arrangement, observe collection and packing, and compare what happened.
rows.pedagogy: Make consequences and trade-offs visible instead of rewarding a guessed correct label.
rows.outcome: Use an observation to explain whether a trial helped and what still needs attention.
rows.evidence: Learner identifies an observed change and an alternative explanation or trade-off.
rows.limits: A successful simulated queue is not workplace competence or proof of every initiative behaviour.
rows.source: Existing market trial/check sequence; step-specific capture pending

rows.title: 06 · Hand over and receive the agreed pay
rows.action: Tell Mara what was tried and found. Complete the agreed job; receive $20 gross − $2 community tax = $18 net plus a crew pass.
rows.pedagogy: Close the work loop with a useful handover while keeping compensation separate from learning judgement.
rows.outcome: Communicate an action, reason and result.
rows.evidence: Decision, explanation and reflection can be evidence; the pay transaction confirms the agreed game job.
rows.limits: Help, retries and mixed results never reduce pay. A reward does not prove mastery.
rows.source: Existing market payment and crew-pass contract; supplied implementation review

rows.title: 07 · Name all five behaviours
rows.action: Use the explicit five-behaviour explanation and source examples; compare the market with other workplaces.
rows.pedagogy: Give precise language after or alongside experience and expose behaviours a single queue cannot demonstrate.
rows.outcome: Distinguish all five official behaviours and explain another example.
rows.evidence: Teacher checks the learner’s own description, including how/why it fits.
rows.limits: Notice / Think / Act / Support / Review is a reflection tool, not the five official behaviours.
rows.source: market-initiative.mjs and initiative-field-guide.html; Carolan printed pp.24–27

rows.title: 08 · Sort a story, get feedback
rows.action: Drag, tap or use the keyboard to match an illustrated workplace story to a behaviour; revise and try the next story.
rows.pedagogy: Provide low-stakes recognition practice with explanatory feedback and accessible controls.
rows.outcome: Identify a plausible behaviour and reconsider an error.
rows.evidence: The quiz/checking activity records practice. Ask for a reason before treating an answer as understanding.
rows.limits: Labels remain visible. Matching and practice stamps are not unaided recall or mastery. No timer or pay penalty.
rows.source: Actual Crew Recall screenshots; market-initiative.mjs

rows.title: 09 · Tell it without the labels
rows.action: Attempt the description/explanation prompts, then explain who could benefit and why.
rows.pedagogy: Move beyond recognition to an explanation the teacher can inspect.
rows.outcome: Explain initiative versus following instructions; justify a second example and a possible benefit.
rows.evidence: Learner’s explanation and reflection, reviewed with feedback; note prompts and support.
rows.limits: An attempted response or coloured sticker does not by itself show accuracy or transfer.
rows.source: Implemented Tell it without the labels / description-explanation practice

rows.title: 10 · Keep the field guide
rows.action: Open the printable guide and the existing shared Initiative one-page resource; use My Life / My work to return.
rows.pedagogy: Give a stable reference for explanation, later retrieval and teacher-supported revision.
rows.outcome: Locate the five behaviours, three possible benefits and retrieval prompts.
rows.evidence: Use a later explanation or saved work artifact; opening/downloading a guide is resource access.
rows.limits: Existing My Work is a destination. Automatic transfer of this new practice into a school portfolio is not established.
rows.source: Actual initiative-field-guide.html; original shared Initiative one-page resource

rows.title: 11 · Review Stats / My collection
rows.action: Inspect the First gig, Story sorter and Tell the story cards, plus the crew pass and collection items.
rows.pedagogy: Make practice visible and offer an encouraging reminder of what to revisit.
rows.outcome: Recognise what was attempted and choose a useful next practice step.
rows.evidence: Game completion and practice counters are signals; inspect the underlying work separately.
rows.limits: The screenshot is a demo review state, not a learner record or an achievement judgement.
rows.source: Actual Stats captures; initiative-progress.mjs / exploration-tools.mjs

rows.title: 12 · Return later with a changed case
rows.action: Teacher schedules retrieval and a different workplace example with less support.
rows.pedagogy: Check retention and transfer beyond the original cues and supported task.
rows.outcome: Independently justify an appropriate initiative action and its limits in a new situation.
rows.evidence: Dated learner explanation/performance and teacher feedback, stored in the chosen portfolio.
rows.limits: Proposed follow-up provision. No automatic timetable, assessment result or classroom completion is claimed.
rows.source: Proposed teacher follow-up; exact curriculum retained

rows.evidence: The supplied screenshots show isolated demo practice.

rows.title: Teacher-reviewed learning status
rows.action: A later design could link a practice signal to an inspected explanation and dated teacher feedback.
rows.pedagogy: Help teacher and student distinguish participation, checking, reviewed evidence and transfer.
rows.outcome: Know which result has actually been reviewed.
rows.evidence: Requires agreed criteria, authorised storage and an implemented evidence bridge.
rows.limits: Proposed addition; no current screenshot or live student-data connection exists in this review.
rows.source: Future evidence design; not a current Stats element

learningPrinciples.purpose: Plan for knowledge students can recall, explain and use beyond the original task. Memory supports understanding and judgement; a memorable activity alone does not demonstrate learning.

core.title: Retrieval practice
core.detail: Make low-stakes recall a regular part of learning: ask students to retrieve an idea, explain it or reconstruct a process before looking at notes. Give corrective feedback, address misconceptions and let them try again.

core.title: Spacing
core.detail: Revisit important learning after a delay and again in later lessons or phases, rather than concentrating all practice in one sitting. Use what students recall and misunderstand to decide the next revisit; the exact schedule depends on the content and learners.

learningPrinciples.selection: Choose supports for the knowledge, task and learner’s current needs, not a fixed visual, auditory or kinaesthetic learning-style label. Explain how to use the strategy and check whether it helps.

options.title: Chunking
options.detail: Group related information into meaningful parts; make the relationships clear, then reconnect the parts in the whole task.

options.title: Meaningful imagery and stories
options.detail: Connect ideas to an accurate concrete image or short story. Check the underlying meaning, not just recall of the picture or plot.

options.title: Memory palace
options.detail: Optionally place a stable list or ordered sequence along familiar imagined locations. Check accurate recall and then teach the explanation and application separately.

options.title: Elaboration and self-explanation
options.detail: Ask why, how, what connects to prior knowledge, and why an example or solution fits. Check and correct the explanation.

options.title: Words plus meaningful diagrams
options.detail: Use labelled diagrams, timelines or flow charts with concise explanation to show relationships and processes; decorative pictures are not the learning goal.

options.title: Interleaving
options.detail: After initial teaching and suitable practice, mix related cases so learners choose and justify the appropriate idea or approach. Avoid random topic switching before foundations are secure.

options.title: Creative rehearsal and memory cues
options.detail: Acrostics, mnemonics, images, drama/role-play, songs and repeated reinforcement are legitimate options when they make the actual curriculum meaningful and memorable. Link the cue to accurate syllabus wording, explanation and workplace application; check whether it helps rather than adding a competing model.

learningPrinciples.cues: Creative memory supports stay optional and purpose-specific. They must reinforce the curriculum’s meaning and application, not become another mandatory assessed list. No particular new song, mnemonic or acrostic is commissioned by this update.
design: State the learning purpose and what successful understanding or performance would look like.

Choose a suitable entry: an informed low-stakes attempt followed by reflection and teaching, or explanation and a worked example first. Scaffold practice, then fade help as learners become ready; make support available again when needed.
Include brief low-stakes recall, corrective feedback and a useful next attempt. A mistake identifies what needs teaching; it is not automatically a summative failure.
Plan later revisits and varied applications across the existing course sequence, rather than treating one completed activity as durable learning.
Ask learners to apply the idea in an authentic task, explain their decision in a different context, and reflect on what changed and what they need next.
learningPrinciples.assessment: Assess accurate reasoning, explanation, application and transfer, not reproduction of a mnemonic alone. Distinguish supported from independent success. Use selected work, demonstration and teacher review; speed, wealth, badges, quiz completion and engagement are not mastery. Retain only the evidence needed under existing privacy and school-use boundaries; this adds no new learner tracking.
learningPrinciples.example: Proposed teaching sequence: after teaching initiative and trying an arrangement at Mara’s market, revisit the five behaviours from memory, check omissions with feedback, then ask which behaviour fits a new workplace situation and why. A later explanation should distinguish initiative from following an instruction and justify the choice. Teacher review considers the reasoning and support used, not the wage or recall score alone.
learningPrinciples.boundary: These are design principles, not a claim of implemented practice or measured Career Empire learning gains. No fixed learning styles or speculative brain mechanism is assumed.

source.title: IES practice guide · Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (2007)
source.scope: Evidence guidance for spacing, retrieval, explanatory questions and purposeful verbal/visual representations; evidence strength and studied contexts vary. Reviewed 21 October 2026.

experience.title: Experience, reflection and explicit teaching
experience.history: The retained sequence is experience → need to learn → supported instruction → application → feedback/consequence → recovery/transfer (8 September 2026 history). V2-D01 (6 September) placed a meaningful encounter before explanation; V2-D18 and the 24 September contract clarify that world events and productive failure are not compulsory for every activity. Direct teaching and EST revision remain legitimate.
experience.experiential: Experiential learning connects doing with reflection: encounter a purposeful situation, notice and discuss what happened, connect it to concepts through explicit explanation, then try again or transfer the learning. Activity or immersion alone is not evidence of understanding.
experience.productive: Productive failure is an optional designed sequence: after access, safety, controls and necessary prerequisites are clear, offer a bounded, low-stakes problem-solving attempt. Compare approaches and reflect, then explicitly explain and consolidate the important ideas with worked examples and solution scaffolding. Follow with supported practice, fading help and a later application or transfer check.
experience.support: Orientation and access support come before an attempt; solution scaffolding can follow it where suitable. Do not withhold essential help, force failure or leave learners struggling without consolidation. Adapt to prior knowledge, task difficulty and accessibility; use teaching or an example first when needed. At Mara’s market, brief the role, safety and workflow first and offer ordinary contextual questions or help on demand. Successful first attempts are valid; early errors guide teaching, not a summative penalty.
experience.source: Existing Kapur (2014) research concerns studied mathematics tasks; it informs a design option, not proof of effectiveness across this course.

initiative.title: Initiative needs explicit teaching
initiative.purpose: The experience alone is not sufficient teaching. The core route must explain all five curriculum behaviours through staged teaching, examples and non-examples, a worked example and consolidation. Optional cards cannot be the only way learners encounter this content. Teach before or after a suitable attempt according to readiness.

behaviours.title: being proactive
behaviours.example: Anticipate confusion and raise a workable idea without waiting for a specific instruction; distinguish this from carrying out a step Mara already prescribed.
behaviours.explained: Introduce initiative versus following an instruction in the purpose/briefing; revisit with a worked market example and debrief.
behaviours.opportunity: Notice an emerging ordering/collection problem and raise a safe suggestion before Mara gives a specific solution. The scenario is assigned practice; that alone is not spontaneous initiative.
behaviours.check: Compare carrying out Mara’s exact instruction with anticipating a need. Explain which shows initiative and why; identify any prompting.
behaviours.state: Required teaching design and planned opportunity/example; not verified runtime provision or learner performance.

behaviours.title: identifying ways to improve current work practices
behaviours.example: Use observations of ordering and collection to propose and test a clearer arrangement, then compare the result.
behaviours.explained: Explicitly connect an observed work practice, proposed change and possible efficiency benefit in the teaching/debrief.
behaviours.opportunity: Observe the baseline, propose a clearer sign/collection arrangement, try it and compare the next customers. Several sensible arrangements may be valid.
behaviours.check: Identify what changed and the observation supporting an improvement; explain why it demonstrates this way rather than merely moving an object.
behaviours.state: Required teaching design and planned opportunity/example; not verified runtime provision or learner performance.

behaviours.title: vocalising your opinions
behaviours.example: Explain a suggested arrangement respectfully to Mara and Sam, with reasons and openness to feedback.
behaviours.explained: Model a respectful opinion with a reason and a non-example that only repeats an instruction.
behaviours.opportunity: Offer Mara/Sam an arrangement or viewpoint, explain the reason, listen and respond to their feedback within the workflow.
behaviours.check: Recognise an opinion being expressed and justify why it is relevant initiative; distinguish a selected label from an explained contribution.
behaviours.state: Required teaching design and planned opportunity/example; not verified runtime provision or learner performance.

behaviours.title: helping fellow workers
behaviours.example: Offer an agreed form of support to Sam when packing or collection needs it; do not bypass safety or the role boundary.
behaviours.explained: Use a concrete Sam/crew-workload example; explain useful support and role/safety limits.
behaviours.opportunity: Notice when Sam needs support, ask what help is useful and offer an agreed packing/collection task. If the runtime does not yet offer this action, illustrate or role-play it and mark it as such.
behaviours.check: Explain how the action helps a fellow worker and why it is appropriate. Distinguish helping from simply reallocating Sam’s job in a menu.
behaviours.state: Required teaching design and planned opportunity/example; not verified runtime provision or learner performance.

behaviours.title: seeking more responsibilities
behaviours.example: Ask to take an appropriate extra role and clarify permission and support; extra work assigned by someone else is not by itself evidence of seeking responsibility.
behaviours.explained: Contrast asking for a suitable extra responsibility with being assigned one; explain permission and support.
behaviours.opportunity: Ask Mara to take an appropriate additional role, such as checking collection for the next wave, with agreed boundaries. Do not treat completing the initially assigned task as seeking more responsibility.
behaviours.check: Identify who initiated the request and explain how it fits this syllabus way. Use another workplace case if the learner did not request a role in the market.
behaviours.state: Required teaching design and planned opportunity/example; not verified runtime provision or learner performance.

initiative.guide: Use the syllabus ways as the core teaching reference. Ask ordinary contextual questions about the actual work: what needs attention, what could improve it, which syllabus way the action demonstrates, why it fits, who may benefit, and what happened. Do not add a named thinking sequence or another list to memorise. Any future optional memory support must reinforce the curriculum wording and demonstrate usefulness.

sequence.title: Clear purpose
sequence.detail: Introduce the concept and purpose: learn how initiative can contribute to the market, not just solve a queue puzzle. Brief role, safety and workflow; make quiet contextual help available. One primary action: begin when ready.

sequence.title: Informed attempt
sequence.detail: Observe, ask or try a bounded arrangement. A successful first attempt is valid. One primary action: review what happened; no forced failure or wrong-button penalty.

sequence.title: Explicit teaching and debrief
sequence.detail: Explain the meaning of initiative, all five syllabus ways and workplace benefits through staged examples and non-examples. Connect justified ways to the learner’s actual actions and results; identify any not yet demonstrated. One primary action: continue after the explanation.

sequence.title: Worked reasoning example
sequence.detail: Show how a queue/collection observation informs a proposal, permission, trial and review. Explain why the action demonstrates a syllabus way and how the workplace may benefit, using ordinary contextual questions. One primary action: try a different case.

sequence.title: New application and feedback
sequence.detail: Use a different workplace scenario; ask which behaviour fits and why. Give corrective feedback and a useful next step, then revisit later. One primary action at a time, no automatic advance.

initiative.evidence: Review the student’s concrete choice, reasoning, observed result and explanation. Distinguish independent from prompted action and initiative from following instructions. An action may demonstrate more than one syllabus way, but not automatically all five. A repeated label, mnemonic, wage, badge, quiz result or opened card is not proof of mastery.
initiative.delivery: Reduce simultaneous instructions and controls: one clear stage and primary action, quiet help on demand, readable/captioned equivalents and deliberate continuation. Scaffold when needed; never withhold access or essential support.
initiative.status: Required Blueprint teaching design/proposal. This page does not claim that the current game’s core route, cards, debrief or assessment has already been changed or validated.
initiative.curriculumScope: Teach the concept, ways of showing initiative and benefits together. The 2027 SCSA Unit 3 Enterprising behaviours content prescribes the five examples below; they are not an ordered taxonomy or five steps to memorise. Understanding and appropriate workplace application matter, not label reproduction alone.
benefits: to create work opportunities (for example, promotion)
initiative.benefitsTeaching: Explain each benefit through the actual action and result: a useful proposal may earn trust or recognition; a clearer collection arrangement may reduce confusion; appropriate contributions may create later work opportunities. These are possible benefits, not guaranteed promotion, rewards or proof of mastery.
initiative.coverageRule: The market must make this content concrete through meaningful examples and opportunities designed around the concept and five syllabus ways, not attach labels to a queue puzzle afterward. Teach and check recognition/explanation across all five. Keep illustrated, practised with help and independently demonstrated claims separate; no single action automatically demonstrates every way.

pilot.title: The opportunity I might miss
pilot.position: An example of the learning loop, not the agreed first chapter or week.
pilot.premise: Avery wants a weekend role helping a community venue. The employer cannot see evidence of teamwork in Avery's first response. The opportunity matters, but the character has a supported chance to revise.
pilot.focus: One job-ad requirement and one evidence-based response. This is not a complete application, full selection-criteria unit or summative assessment.
detailFocus: Identify the selected requirement in a job advertisement.
Use STAR (situation, task, action, result) for one response; SAO and CAR remain for later teaching.
Communicate relevant evidence to the intended employer.
pilot.choices: Choose between two fictional roles with the same learning demand, then choose a truthful example from school, home, volunteering or a supplied fictional case. Paid-work experience is not required.
pilot.safeStakes: The first response is returned for clarification. No real countdown, public failure ranking, permanent career lockout or loss of friendship/health points. Pause and retry remain possible.
pilot.fun: A role the player actually wants, a character who responds to their choices, visible improvement after a retry and a small optional original noticeboard joke. The appeal is agency and discovery, not a quiz with decorative travel.

beats.title: Something I want
beats.player: Choose a role and notice the opportunity it could open for Avery.
beats.teacher: Introduce the fictional setting and confirm the shared learning focus; offer a ready-made character.
beats.evidence: The chosen role and a short reason. Engagement information only.

beats.title: My first response is not enough
beats.player: Inspect the ad and try a short response. The employer asks: 'What did you actually do?'
beats.teacher: Observe what students notice before instruction. Do not grade the first attempt as a penalty.
beats.evidence: Save the first attempt and the requirement the student selected.

beats.title: Now I need the technique
beats.player: Compare a vague claim with a specific example; learn STAR and identify its four parts.
beats.teacher: Give explicit instruction, model one response and check understanding. Supply text and spoken alternatives.
beats.evidence: A brief practice response and feedback identifying the next improvement.

beats.title: Make a stronger case
beats.player: Write or dictate a new response, select relevant evidence and explain why it fits the requirement.
beats.teacher: Check relevance, the student's own contribution and the stated outcome. A sentence frame supports students who need it.
beats.evidence: Revised response, matched requirement and short explanation of the change.

beats.title: See what changed, then recover
beats.player: Receive a specific acknowledgement or a clear next revision. Revise without losing access to the opportunity.
beats.teacher: Review the response as meets / developing / needs support. Any future automatic checks assist, not replace, teacher judgement.
beats.evidence: Teacher review, feedback and any retry. Story acknowledgement is provisional, not an automatic cash award.

beats.title: Could I do this somewhere else?
beats.player: Match the approach to a different fictional ad and name one strategy worth keeping.
beats.teacher: Check transfer and ask whether the player cared about improving. Note confusion, friction and support needed.
beats.evidence: Exit response and a separate engagement observation. This does not establish whole-unit mastery.

proof.check: The response addresses the chosen requirement, identifies the student's action and gives a relevant outcome.
proof.method: Compare first and revised responses using a teacher-agreed rubric; include a different-ad exit check.
proof.threshold: Tania must set the pilot success threshold before classroom testing.

proof.check: The player can explain what they wanted, chooses to improve after feedback and notices a consequence.
proof.method: Observe voluntary revision, confusion and off-task friction; ask a short private reflection. Time on screen alone is not success.
proof.threshold: Agree observation criteria with Tania; no arbitrary retention target is claimed.

proof.check: The same learning can be completed without 3D navigation, paid-work history or timed pressure.
proof.method: Test keyboard, reduced motion, text alternative, pause/resume and absence/catch-up on target school devices.
proof.threshold: No learner is blocked from the required learning; unresolved access failures block release.

proof.check: Attempts, review and progress belong to the right student and class and survive resume.
proof.method: Test save/reload, identity, permissions, teacher review and repeat submissions with fictional accounts.
proof.threshold: No lost evidence, cross-student exposure or duplicate reward transaction in the agreed checks.

definitionOfDone: Approved scope or explicitly labelled proposal; evidence linked.
Implementation, deployment, testing and Tania acceptance individually recorded.

retainedPrinciples: Learning is experienced, not merely tested.
The Career Learning Cycle drives the experience.
The player builds a life, not selects one fixed future.
Choices produce visible and meaningful consequences.
Growth changes both the learner and the world.
Career plans are provisional and adaptability is normal.
Success is broader than income, grades or occupational prestige.
Failure creates learning and recovery, not humiliation or permanent exclusion.
Every curriculum requirement is deliberately mapped and evidenced.
Students receive repeated opportunities to improve and demonstrate achievement.
Individual agency and collective responsibility coexist.
Classroom usability, inclusion and accessibility are design requirements.
The opening shows intriguing possibility, not finished abundance.
Only approved, bounded work moves into production.

st4sReadiness.title: School Deployment, Security, Privacy & ST4S Readiness

governingSource.notes: Guide pp.10–11 readiness list uses parent C/P references, duplicates AI_PR3 and prints AI_5; use detailed AI_T5 and include AI_PR2/AI_SF6A from detailed criteria. No silent omitted control. Question excerpts are locators; full source tier/response columns govern.

statusDefinitions.PASS—VERIFIED: Applicable requirement satisfied for exact scope by current validated evidence; never inferred from provider marketing.
statusDefinitions.LIKELY PASS: Plausible but incomplete proof. Blocks readiness.
statusDefinitions.GAP: Observed missing/unsafe control; source gap may be established while deployed state remains unknown. Blocks readiness.
statusDefinitions.N-A: Documented source-specific non-applicability approved with evidence/date/reviewer. Not a PASS.
statusDefinitions.UNVERIFIED: Unknown configuration, applicability or evidence. Blocks readiness.

tier.candidate: Tier 2 educational game/career guidance only; not a confirmed classification
tier.rationale: P9 data and P10 functionality determine tier. LMS/analytics/two-way communication/payment/file-hosting features may change scope; review full product, not only 3D route.

questions.data: What data is collected or processed, for what purpose, and which fields are personal, sensitive, inferred or optional?
questions.locations: Where are live data, backups, logs, metadata, disaster recovery, test and development data stored AND processed?
questions.accessCountries: Who can access the data, including support, administrators and contractors, and from which countries?
questions.providers: Which third parties/subprocessors receive which data and under which contracts and change-notice terms?
questions.lifecycle: What are retention periods, deletion propagation (including backups), export and termination procedures?
questions.encryption: What encryption and key-management settings protect each transport hop and stored copy?
questions.logging: What is logged, redacted, retained and auditable; who can read/export logs and respond to alerts?
questions.identity: What authentication, MFA, RBAC, session/revocation, password and recovery controls are enforced server-side?
questions.isolation: How is school/class/student isolation enforced and negatively tested against identifier/role tampering?
questions.privacySafety: What privacy, consent, accessibility and student-safety implications, threats and mitigations change?
questions.applicability: Does the ST4S tier, control set, AI module, jurisdiction or conditional evidence applicability change?
questions.verification: Which implementation checks, tests, evidence, policies, diagrams and documentation must be updated?

guardrails: Minimise personal and sensitive data; use synthetic records in development and test. Pseudonyms remain personal when linkable.
Enforce hard school/tenant isolation on the server, database, storage, functions, caches, exports and logs.
Default deny, least privilege and trusted immutable membership; never trust client role, school or student identifiers.
No cross-school discovery by default. Any aggregate comparison needs documented purpose, small-cell protection and security/privacy approval.
Avoid unnecessary student communication/social features; teacher moderation does not replace access control or safety incident handling.
Student-facing AI requires explicit recorded architecture and security approval, privacy/safety assessment, model/provider evidence and AI control applicability review before enablement.
Verify Australian storage AND processing across every component and access country; a database region alone is insufficient.
Never infer compliance from a vendor/product name. Verify deployed configuration, data flows, contracts/subprocessors, operational processes and evidence.

backlog.title: Replace browser-side student authentication and weak password handling
backlog.remediation: Replace client SHA-256 comparison/readable password_hash with server-side managed authentication or a narrowly scoped authenticated session broker. Use a slow salted password KDF if custom auth remains, CSPRNG credentials, rate limits and uniform login errors; revoke direct anonymous credential access. Revoke sessions on reset/deactivation.
backlog.validation: Synthetic student A cannot read any credential hash or impersonate B by altering storage/IDs; brute-force/reset/revocation tests pass.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Local source available; deployment and authenticated configuration remain unverified.

backlog.title: Make tenant membership trusted and immutable to ordinary users
backlog.remediation: Replace school membership inferred from user-editable teachers.school_id with verified immutable auth-subject membership approved by a school administrator. Lock membership/role columns; enforce tenant-consistent foreign keys and class assignment, and eliminate prototype permissive policies.
backlog.validation: Two synthetic schools; attempted self-reassignment, foreign student/class IDs, revoked staff, RPC and direct REST all denied.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Local source available; deployment and authenticated configuration remain unverified.

backlog.title: Isolate feedback and moderation data
backlog.remediation: Replace feedback school IDs embedded in untrusted message JSON with server-bound non-null tenant columns. Remove null-school visibility to all authenticated teachers; unaffiliated reports go only to restricted triage. Scope reviewer roles and immutable audit logs; limit anonymous submission and sanitise inputs.
backlog.validation: Anonymous submission cannot forge tenant identity; malformed/missing school IDs never broaden read access; raw responses visible only to authorised reviewers.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Local source available; deployment and authenticated configuration remain unverified.

backlog.title: Disable default cross-school discovery and validate aggregation
backlog.remediation: Disable anonymous Global Index school/class summaries by default. Any approved cross-school comparison must remove class codes, enforce participation/role controls and minimum cohort thresholds; assess re-identification.
backlog.validation: Unauthenticated and school-A accounts cannot enumerate school-B class codes, small cohorts or identifiable records.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Local source available; deployment and authenticated configuration remain unverified.

backlog.title: Inventory and verify deployed Supabase configuration
backlog.remediation: Obtain read-only project metadata and catalog export; reconcile to source. Inventory all tables/fields/views/materialized views, auth metadata categories, RLS/grants, extensions, triggers/functions, buckets/policies, Edge Functions, webhooks, scheduled jobs, replicas, log drains and backups.
backlog.validation: Signed deployment/schema comparison and component data-flow inventory; no real record dump required.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Primary project identity and ap-southeast-2 region observed live; deeper dashboard stalled. Authenticated Supabase project metadata/region; read-only database catalogs and settings; bucket/function manifests; redacted logs; project membership and support-access attestations; backup/PITR and restore receipts.

backlog.title: Prove residency, support access and provider assurance
backlog.remediation: Record live, backup, log, metadata, DR/test/dev and Edge execution countries; remote support/admin access countries; full chain of subprocessors and relocation-notice lead times. Collect current in-scope IRAP/SOC2 Type II/ISO27001 proof for every component. Where Australian-only requirements cannot be met, restrict/disable the component or obtain a school-approved compliant deployment plan before migration. A second paused project is visible in the same organisation in ap-northeast-1; establish whether it holds related historical data and any migration/deletion obligations without assuming a connection.
backlog.validation: H1/H2 country matrix, H5 enforceable notification workflow, H6 component coverage and school-specific acceptance signed off.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Primary project identity and ap-southeast-2 region observed live; deeper dashboard stalled. Actual project region/settings; signed current DPA/subprocessor list and support access terms; log/backups/CDN/SMTP contracts; H6 reports; school risk report and hosting conditions.

backlog.title: Review auth configuration, MFA and recovery
backlog.remediation: Verify organisation/admin MFA, invitations, trusted teacher onboarding, RBAC, email verification, password policy, reset-token expiry/single use, redirect allowlist, enumeration/rate limits and session lifetime/invalidation. Enforce server-side rather than UI-only school/email checks.
backlog.validation: Synthetic role/recovery matrix and reviewed redacted settings export.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Local source available; deployment and authenticated configuration remain unverified.

backlog.title: Define retention/deletion/export and test full restoration
backlog.remediation: Replace login deactivation/anonymised login labels as a substitute for full deletion. Define per-category retention and school-record obligations; cover Auth, responses/reviews, storage, logs, local caches, backups and recipients. Implement authorised export/deletion and resurrection controls; test restore including storage objects.
backlog.validation: Isolated synthetic full restore and deletion/export propagation receipts, RPO/RTO and backup-expiry evidence.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Local source available; deployment and authenticated configuration remain unverified.

backlog.title: Minimise free text, progress profiles and browser persistence
backlog.remediation: Classify student/staff identifiers, responses/feedback and inferred profiles. Treat wellbeing/financial values as simulated only after verifying provenance; free text may contain sensitive disclosures. Remove unnecessary identity duplication, bound offline persistence, isolate users and clear shared-device data on logout.
backlog.validation: Field/purpose inventory plus shared-device logout, retention and cross-account browser tests.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Local source available; deployment and authenticated configuration remain unverified.

backlog.title: Inventory integrations, downloads, analytics and supply chain
backlog.remediation: Map Supabase, hosting/CDN, SMTP/SSO, external media/docs, telemetry and any export endpoints. Pin/bundle external JavaScript with integrity review (current Supabase loader uses mutable @2 CDN URL); review browser permissions, file MIME/size/malware checks and log redaction.
backlog.validation: Dependency/endpoint inventory, vulnerability scan, permission and download review, no unapproved student-data egress.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Local source available; deployment and authenticated configuration remain unverified.

backlog.title: Review classroom communication, boards, safety and AI applicability
backlog.remediation: Review student responses, teacher feedback, community votes/boards, leaderboards, reflections and wellbeing-themed mechanics; minimise communication, document moderation/report/escalation and staff-student contact rules. Verify all runtime/backend AI pathways before a reasoned AI N-A; authoring AI and simulated AI-themed gameplay do not alone establish student-facing AI.
backlog.validation: Safety misuse tests, moderation audit trail and signed complete feature/tier/AI applicability review.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Local source available; deployment and authenticated configuration remain unverified.

backlog.title: Confirm payments and app/extension applicability
backlog.remediation: Verify shop uses only simulated currency and no card/payment processor across all services. Verify whether native/mobile/desktop/extension builds exist and requested permissions. Record reasoned N-A only with evidence.
backlog.validation: Reviewed complete product inventory and synthetic transaction/permission inspection.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Local source available; deployment and authenticated configuration remain unverified.

backlog.title: Assign operational owners and prepare final school/privacy documents
backlog.remediation: Nominate qualified security/privacy and safeguarding owners; finalise privacy/collection notices, terms, incident notification, training/offboarding, BCP/DR and shared patching responsibilities. Obtain WA public-school risk assessment/catalogue entry and school approval/consent/treatments; separately establish CEWA/ECC requirements.
backlog.validation: Authorised final documents, tabletop and training/access review, school-specific written approval.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Organisation identity/ABN, owner nominations, policy approvals, staff-only WA catalogue/risk report and school/sector requirements.

backlog.title: Independent pre-submission assurance
backlog.remediation: Commission scoped vulnerability assessment, independent penetration test, independent privacy/document review, evidence audit and mock Readiness Check of exact candidate. Fix and retest findings; preserve reports and assessor independence.
backlog.validation: All applicable controls verified, no open blocking findings, final evidence current and mock Ready; authorised submission receipt afterward.
backlog.evidenceRequired: Authorised test scope/accounts and independent qualified reviewers; vendor/hosting testing permission as needed.
